blocks.x: I can remember years ago my daddy used to play in what was it?
Sturryville.
Yeah, he played in Sturryville. Well I was wondering, first of all, do you remember about how old he was when he died and the date that he died?
My father was 52 years old and he died November 23rd, 1933. 33.
You don't remember his exact birthday I guess?
Yes, October 26th.
Oh, it's when he was born.
What year would that be?
We can figure it up. We can subtract that all right. It's all we have. I'm sorry, I took your chair.
October 26th was his birth date. That's the birth date.
What did you tell me about your father when you tell your mother to come get the money?

Oh, my daddy would tell her to come meet him at the place where he worked and she would go on there to meet him and he wouldn't be there. And the next couple of days she would get a letter from him. He was in Tennessee or some other place. He had gone and taken another job. Yeah. She wouldn't know a thing about it.
You mentioned a few minutes ago that he played in a lot of circus bands.

Oh, he traveled with Barnum and Bailey's circus for five years from 1907 until 1912. And he played on the Steamer Capitol. I have here the funeral parades with Manuel Perez. I remember him telling me an incident where when he was playing at Tom Anderson's, they paid him $10 to blow when day is done on his mouthpiece. Without the trumpet?
Without the instrument.
Without the instrument.
Do you remember, did he usually use a trumpet or a carnet that's a little bit shorter? A carnet. It was usually the carnet. In the beginning.
But when he died, he had a trumpet.
So that time he changed.
But years, all the years before that he had a carnet. He always called it a carnet.
Is that a list that he made out that you had?

No, no. That's just little things that I remembered about him. Oh, that's wonderful. My mother, I told him I would do that. My mother always told me that he played his first solo when he was 18 years old at the Old Globes Hall. Oh yes. I don't know where that is.
That was down by, near the auditorium. That's right. Somewhere in that section. St. Claude and St. Peter and all in there. Yeah, somewhere in that section.
And I remember him playing on a roof garden.
That's the one, the Pythian Temple, the one up by the city hall now, up in that section. That's the roof garden. Yeah.
And what else is that? All the carnival parades.
Oh yes. Do you remember which bands did he play with Manuel Perez on that or some of the other bands?
The funerals he played with Manuel Perez, but the carnival parades he played with Jake Steve.
Jake Steve? Mm-hmm.
Jake Steve's band. I heard of all bands. The Maccabees. They were called the Maccabees.
I never knew, I haven't heard of them.
Well that's him. I'm sure if you would find someone who's connected with Jake Steve.
We probably will run into someone sooner or later.
He'll tell you about Jake Steve. My daddy played a long time with Jake Steve. What did Jake Steve play?
Did he play? Yes, he played an instrument. I can't remember which one.

But he was at, he was, that was the name of the band. He was an electromeda. Yes, at the time he was, in fact he and my daddy, sometimes when he couldn't take over, my daddy would take over. That's how they would alternate.
You remember, was it a colored band or a white band? Because I understand your father played with some white bands.
Jake Steve was a white band.
That's what I thought it might be.
He played, oh my daddy played with all kinds of bands. Just all, anybody that had, was ready to have him, he played. He just didn't stop at anything.

By the way, do you know where he had his lessons or if he, who he studied with, the name of a teacher or if he went to a certain school or anything? That I can't remember. Did he ever tell you anything about that?

I can't remember. All I can remember, my mother telling me about him being 18 years old. When he had his first solo. When he played his first solo at the Globe's Hall. I can remember that. But, I don't remember who he studied under. But he did study under someone. He had to, to know music like he knew it. He really, he was really a good musician. He can tell you that.
When y'all was living on some foot, do you remember what, the job he was playing? He was playing one of those taxi dances.
He used to play on Canal Street. Yeah. Canal between Villery and.
Between Villery and Murray.
Yeah, he played that.
And he'd go out to the Jump Hotel on that side of the bank.
Uh huh. Jitney dancing. Do you remember what that was, Darryl?

I forgot, I forgot the name of the place, but I had my band in there once. In fact, it was my band and it was James Davis's job and he took my band in there. And after he got on his feet, you know, I'm out. You know how that goes.
Do you remember that place Shakey or another?

It wasn't the Hummer Boogie. No, the Hummer Boogie was in the district. This was on Canal on that side. How old is it? It was just like, you know, like if you would walk in an apartment house, that's the way that you're walking at it. It was a big dance hall. Oh, yes. A big beautiful stage and everything. Yeah. You know, Jitney's Jitney dance. A Jitney dance.
Yeah. And paid 10 cents a day.

The music box was on Canal. And Carondelet. Yeah. Right where Stein's Clown's story. Because I played the Crescent Billion Hall across the street a couple of nights with P. Roy and I played there with Walter P. Sean. My daddy used to play with P. Roy. Yeah.
I have a little note here where he played at Soldiers Field in Chicago. In Chicago. Mm-hmm. And he also played at the Farmers Band, but I don't remember the name, but it was in 1970.
And Soldiers Field, I think, was pretty late, wasn't it?
Soldiers Field, that wasn't too long before he died.
No, because I think they built that shortly before the World's Fair up there.
That's when I'm, he died in 33. 33. And that was about, oh, I'd say about five years before he died.
Do you remember which band he was with when he went to Chicago at that time? Did he put it, a dance band or a brass?
No, it was a brass band.
Circus band or something?
Brass band. Because he, my mother has a picture of him in that band. That was also a white band.
Mm-hmm.
And I'm trying to think of the artists. He, he played the Steamer Capitol. Oh, yes.
Do you remember whose band that was? Was that his own band or somebody like Pierone or?
No, I think that was just a group of men he got together. Mm-hmm. And, you know, they played in other words. The Steamer Capitol. He was the leader of that band. Yes. But there was no name to it.
Yes, usually the cornettists was the leader of the chorus group.

Just a group of men that they played there. Mm-hmm. And I've mentioned the roof guard. I think there's, you know, another place he played? I don't know how prominent a place it was, but it was a citrus garden. I don't know, that was in the country someplace. He played there quite a while. You played, did you ever play there?
Down in, down in, down in Bureus. Bureus, that's it. They have a big, uh, Orange Festival every, about October. That's it. In Bureus.
Oh, yeah. They used to go there every evening. That's where it was. In Bureus. Uh-huh. Or, that's the Orange Grove, huh?
Something about the Orange Festival.

At that time, at that time, it just started at 8, to get to Bureus there to leave you about 2, 3 and even if they were riding, unless you catch the little train at Canal and River. You just come all the way to Canal and River and have a little train. Right. But if you go in the car, it would take you 3 to 4 hours to get the Bureus down the road, you know what I'm saying?
Now, another thing I remember about him when Lois Armstrong was leaving here to go to Chicago. Wasn't it Chicago?
Yeah. Yes.
He asked my daddy to go with him.
He did, man.
He said, if we do well, we'll stay, and if we don't, we'll come back. But my daddy wouldn't leave. But Lois Armstrong went on.
You mentioned that your father helped him with some harmony or some kind of music?
He taught him harmony. Taught him harmony.
Harmony, yeah.
He had a large book, and he, several times, lots of times, he'd come home and my daddy would teach him that.
Did he bring his coronet with him or? Oh, yes.
Always had his instrument with him. I was quite a little girl, but I remember him.
I mean, can you tell us anything about, I know you can, about your father, about how tall he was? Was he, he looks rather small on the pictures? He is, he was short.
My daddy was about five, what would I be, about five, three, huh? Three or four.
I suppose.
That's about like, just about five.
He wasn't much taller than you or any taller? No, no.
I'm about, I'm about, same height. Same height. Same height.

We might confirm about this picture because, as I say, some people have tried to tell me that that was Peter Bocos or somebody else. No, that's my daddy. The picture, this is one taken to Tom Anderson's, is that right?
Tom Anderson's Canal and Ramport.
Paul Barbrin has a copy of the picture too. And we had borrowed one from Witten Joe Nicholas, the uncle of Albert Nicholas. And then this is Willie San Diego and Louis Russell, I believe, on piano.
I never knew the two that was playing. I remember the name now, Russell. Yes.
My daddy used to speak of him.
He came from Panama.
He used to play with Armstrong. He traveled with Louis Armstrong until about 1945, I believe.
That's a perfect picture of him. Yes, it's him. That looks just like him, you say. And that other one is a good picture. It's quite clear.
This one here. You see, Gnardham and Pete, you know who that is.
You have the other one in the house?
Yeah, right here.
That's probably a trumpet I think he was playing there. It looks like that.
Yeah, that's a great trumpet.
It's a pity you couldn't get this one with him blowing.
Yes, this one is very dim.
Mm-hmm.
We might try to...
And this is another good picture of him. It's not in uniform there, but that's a good one.
The other man on this picture, what is his name again? Conyers.
Ledger Conyers. Ledger Conyers.
Conyers.
C-U-D-G-E-R. Ledger.
C-L-N-U-S. And he was a friend of yours too, Harold. Oh, my dad's personal friend, Harold.
He's dead.
Let's see if there's any date. There's no date on this Tom Anderson picture, I believe.
No, but that's in the 20s, I can tell you.

I think so, it's about the early 20s, I believe. Early 20s, yeah. Because Barbara and Albert Nicholas went to Chicago again around 1925 or so, I think, and stayed up there. So that would have to be before...
It was in the 20s.
Before 1925, I think.
Yeah.
I noticed on this one, he seems to be playing into a microphone. I wonder, did you know where that was taken? No, I really don't.
I don't know where it was. Was that real small one?
Is the microphone?
It was a band though, because you can see the piano. Look, the piano. Yeah, that's right.
Oh yeah, that's got the whole band.
And here's another fellow right on the side with his arm there. Yeah, somebody had a...
What band?
It looks like a microphone. It's something up here. Peter?
No, you talk about sweet trumpet. Oh, sweet.
Oh man, it's a great trumpet.
Didn't he blow a trumpet? Oh, just like Harry James. The other people have told us here, wonderful tone. I mean, that wonderful tone, man.
Yeah, when he would blow an instrument, it actually looked like the words were coming out.
Looked like he was singing to you.
That's right.
He'd blow them out.
You know what was wonderful? I guess I must have been a little girl about, oh, about nine years old. And my daddy used to have Albert Glenny and...who was daddy called? MacNeil.
Yeah.
Thomas MacNeil. Wendell MacNeil was his name. Wendell MacNeil. And my daddy and Albert Glenny. And they used to wake us up with serenaders. Two o'clock in the morning.
I thought I needed to win that phrase.
Right under the window.
Is he a guitar player, MacNeil? No, violinist. Violin, I forgot.
He's in Chicago. I don't know if he's living or not. That's where he went to.
When I was a little kid, I was playing with Woody Symphony.
At MacNeil, yeah.
Uh-huh.

He played a sweet violin. But that was so sweet. You know, in the early hours of the morning, and they had their mutes. My daddy would use the mute in his horn. Yeah. And that was so sweet to hear that music at two o'clock in the morning. I never did forget that.
What kind of pieces were they? Something slow or what were they like? Do you remember what?
I don't remember.
Popular songs or something?
Well, it would be something popular of the time, you know. But I can't remember just what pieces he played. But his favorite, my daddy's favorite piece was Night and Day.
Really Night and Day.

And, uh, Come to, uh, what is it? Oh, Come to Me? Yeah. Oh, Come to Me. Always on the Eyes. Oh, Come to Me. He used to love to play that. He played that with that mute. And, uh, and, um, uh, what was the name of that piece again? I can't think of it. As much as I'd like to say it. Our Sweet Mystery of Life. Oh, yeah.
The Victor Herbert, I used to play that. Oh, yeah. My daddy played.
Well, I used to play the piano. Why is it then? And we used to play together.
By the way, where did you take lessons? And who was your teacher? Did your father help you any?
Oh, my father helped me, yes. To learn to read music. But I was taught by Valerie. Boy, she's dead. She was my teacher. And, uh, well, you know, he used to give me hints.
Did you ever play in any orchestras when you were younger?
We had a little neighborhood band. And, uh, Harold, you remember the boys. Peter DePass. Oh, yeah. And, uh, Alvarez Perez. Yeah. And I used to play the piano.
Peter DePass played the trumpet.
Elliot Taylor.
Elliot Taylor. Very fine. Very fine.
Very fine. Very fine.
Very fine.
Very fine. Yeah, Barney. You know, you can play with us. Oh.
But just another neighborhood. Alvarez Perez. Saxophone. Saxophone. Yeah, that's Matt Perez's son.
That's Matt Perez's son. Yeah, that's Matt Perez's son.
He's in California now. Yes, that's right. He's brother Dodge, you know, who played trumpet. Yeah. Yeah, that's the one I met at Chicago.
I remember that in that first time.

Peter DePass, would he be, uh... Peter DePass. Oh, that's no relation to... D-E-P-S-S. It's D-E-P-S. It's D-E-P-S. It's no relation to Arnold DePass. No. He's the drummer Arnold DePass. Arnold DePass was a drummer drummer.
My dad used to play with Arnold DePass.
Yeah.
But that was just a little neighborhood, uh... Yeah. We used to play for ourselves, you know, our own entertainment. But they got a few jobs out of town, but my mother wouldn't let me go.
Well, I played a few jobs with Pete.
Well, I had stopped playing with him.
I used to go to rehearsal with him, and I said, Peter, and you have to talk to him next to the speakeasy where I was playing at night, by Zanko. Yeah. Right next to his house. Yeah.
That's what I did. You know who used to come in our house and practice a lot, too? Uh, he's dead now. Eddie, um... I remember the last husband.
Eddie Pearson.
Eddie Pearson.

Well, Eddie Pearson was our first drummer player. We first met. I was not with the moon I was sitting there. I remember we got to get a bigger job. Eddie Pearson was a little motorboat. He was playing drum over us. He was there on St. Anne between Johnson and Galvis. Yeah. When he was driving a little truck with a seat off, plays on Decatur Charter.
Yeah.
That's right.

Well, he used to come around home and we, you know, he used to have his band come and practice. Well, they didn't have a name either, but just a group of boys that would get together and play. Played some nice music. And he did well because, uh, Eddie really ended up...
Well, Eddie was a fine drummer player. A wonderful tone. I mean, he ended up with a different drummer up there. Yeah.
I doubt if I could play any piano anymore.
Oh, you haven't played recently? No.

I haven't played in years. Oh, that's pretty good. But my daddy and I used to play together. I had, um, a book of, uh, carnet and piano solos. He would play, you know, the leads and I would accompany him. And we made one little record of, uh, Oh Lovely Night. Oh, you did? Uh huh. And, uh, is that...
What happened to that?
No, no.
The record is gone. That's too bad.

You know how you used to buy the little discs and you'd put it right at home and we made it together? Wow. And Tales from Huffman. We made that. We used to play all the time. Good music. And Balsays from Jocelyn. Oh yeah. Used to play that. All those good numbers.
I was gonna ask, before I forget it, uh, did any of your uncles, did your father have any brothers that played?
No. He was the only one.
The only one. And did his father play any instrument, do you know?
No. Uh, yes, I think he did. He played the guitar. But I think more so for himself. Just, uh, you know, to amuse himself. He didn't go out and make a living at it like my father did.
Do you remember? That's your grandfather. Do you remember him? Oh, yes. Do you remember? What was his first name?
Eusebio.
How was that again?
E-U-S-E-B-I-O.
That's a usual name for me.
I have a brother named Eusebio. He's named after him. Uh-huh. And I have two brothers and three sons and none of them play music. Oh. None of them.
I was going to ask if your father left his trumpet to one of the sons or something and they kept
on?
We had it.
You had it for a while. And my mother, I don't know, somehow got away from her. I don't know what she did with it. But, uh, my dad was a pretty good musician.

People have told me that he was famous for not using any pressure, what they call a non-pressure system. That's right. He told me once that he could tie a string, hang the trumpet down, say from the light or someplace, and walk up to it without touching it, and play get high C on it just by touching it. That's right. Did you ever see him demonstrate anything like that?
Yes. And, uh, you never see this swell on my dad.
Never puffed out his cheeks. Never.
All from here. He used to teach that to his students, too.
Oh, did he teach many students?
Oh, yeah. He had quite a bit of students. Yeah. Quite a bit of young men. He taught, and I don't know where they are. They all, you know, gone away.
I will run into a few. I think I have talked to maybe one or two people that say they had some lessons from him. Uh-huh.
Of course, our- Well, my daddy taught Albert Nicholas.
Albert Nicholas, too.
He taught Albert Nicholas. When, uh, when Albert came out of the Navy, he came right to my farm.
Did he bring his clarinet, too, or was it mostly for reading, or to learn the instrument?

He was to learn, uh, I think it was for the reading. Uh-huh. To analyze the music, you know? Uh-huh. I think that's what it was. I know he taught him. Yeah. Because he used to come twice a week for lessons. Yeah. And we were living on St. Philip Street that day. Uh-huh. You knew when, when we lived there. Where were you at the time when we lived on St. Philip?

Well, I was a good boy, but I was gone. Oh, I've been gone. Every time a band came, I was gone. That's why I figured you were so much, uh- Yeah, you see, when I was small, when we lived around, I was playing on the steam and wash it's called, but Lewis Andre was living next to Peter Flair, next to Santa Hans Church. Who? Lewis Andre was a kid that died just for the sites for us in Philadelphia. I remember. He lived across the street from, uh, the boy pals and, um, he was- I can't remember. He was, uh, when he came out of the book, I took that job, and I stayed on that, and from one thing to another, you know, kept going.
My daddy used to play all out in Chicago and, um, South Carolina. Anywhere. Just anywhere. He traveled all over. A lot of travel.
I was gonna ask if you remember hearing in practice. Did he ever practice at home? Yes. About how long would he practice, and do you know what he played?
He practiced every day. Every day?
Every day. Oh, there's a ball we can stop.
Every day my daddy practiced. Oh, he practiced the triple tongue. Yeah. Well, he was one.

Did you ever hear him do that? Yes, indeed. I've heard he was very wonderful at triple tongue. Yes, he would really play that. Did he practice scales and other things too, or mostly on pieces, or what would he do?

Scales, always before he started to play anything, he'd run his scales all the time. And he did the same thing with his students and that. They had to do that scale work. In other words, he said you just can't keep up without your scale work. Right. He could run those scales and triple tongue. I used to love to hear him play High Society. Did you ever hear him play that? Yeah.
Everything. Man Perez. Man Perez. He and Man Perez had nothing trouble playing around there. He could play the High Society and make the clarinet. You remember Sidney Bean?
Oh, yeah. He played the clarinet. He died too. He was a very good clarinet.
Very good clarinet. Sidney Bean.
Sidney Bean.
Sidney Bean. Sidney Bean.
Sidney Bean.
Uh-huh. Simeon. Well, it was A number one, she called me. A number one kind of players. Those were good musicians.
And you never hear them mentioned. No. They're not being mentioned.
I guess they don't- They're gonna be mentioned.
I'm gonna dig them.
At least we're getting some of the information down now. Harold's been very kind to help us find you and some other people too we're going to look up.
That's about, I can't remember too many, I guess every now and then you know something that comes to you.
Yes, naturally, it's hard to remember back your whole lifetime in a short-
It's quite a few years. My father's dead now, 26 years. Yes, going on 26 years, 27. He died in 33. In November, this coming November will be 37 years he's dead.
Did he play right up to the last, do you remember? Or did he do?

To the very last. The doctor told him to stay in bed. And he was so weak. And he said, told my mother, he said, I'm going for one last job. And different people told my mother that that night he played so beautiful that it looked like it, he knew it was his last time to play. And I think it was a week or 10 days afterwards he died. He actually played to the last. He believed in that horn. That's like I said.
Every way you see him he had it on his arm.
He had it on his arm.
You know, he used a very similar music occasionally, having a sack. Yes, he used to use it on his arm. Every way you see him, all day or night.
He had it on his arm. That was part of his life. He really loved that instrument.
You were speaking about him practicing. Did he ever practice with just the mouthpiece? Yes.
You were saying he played on the mouthpiece. Lots of times.
He practiced just the mouthpiece.

Just with his mouthpiece and then afterwards he put it on the horn. Yeah. Wash out that horn and then put it in stop with that triple tongue. That was another habit every day. He practiced that triple tongue. I don't know for what reason. He would never pick up that horn without the Carnival of Venice. It was his very, you know, his favorite piece for triple tongue. That's what he used to play.
He used to play all these variations and all the fancy variations. Yeah.
You know in the Carnival of Venice there's a lot of variations. Played all of that. I wish I could think up some more.
I'm trying to think if there's anything else we could ask. There's nothing else about his family that you could tell? Anyone else that was musical in the family?
No other than myself. We were the only two that played, you know that.
And his father as you say played guitar.
Yeah. Guitar, yeah. That's about the only one in the family that played. I started off my oldest son with a horn and he practiced about a year.
Did your mother play any musical instrument or sing or anything? Sing.

She would sing. She had a very nice voice. She had a very nice voice. But she didn't sing out with it. It was just amuse herself. Yes. But she does have a very nice voice. Mommy. At least she had. My mother's 77 now. Getting long in years. And my father would be 78 if he was little.
He wouldn't be so awfully old either.
No, he could have been here. He died quite young.
52 years old. Some people keep on playing until they're old. Sure. Old man Glennie did I guess. Until he was in his 80's he could still play. Yeah.
I knew him well.
Piku still plays. Yes, that's right. He's over 80.
That's another man my father used to play with. He knows my daddy well.
Yes, I think he's mentioned him when we talked to him. I'm quite sure he talked to him.
And you know who my daddy used to play with? A lot. Celestine.
Oh yes, Celestine.
Yeah. Played a lot with him. In other words, I don't know whether they, who was the leader. But I know they played, didn't he play a trumpet?
Oh yes, he played trumpet too.
If I can remember correctly, my father used to tell me that he played the second.
Yes, I usually used two trumpets in his back.
He was first and Celestine was second.
Good.
There's another one. Every now and then something comes back.
Did he ever mention the Tio's? Yes, Lorenzo Tio. And then there were two older, Papa Tio and Lorenzo Senior, I think they called him.
Yes, my father knew all the Tio's. He knew all of them. They were very friendly with each other.
They were all music teachers too, I guess. Yes.
So you could have known them. All the Tio's. There's one that lived right here on London Avenue. That's the one I was telling you about this morning, about the Duke of Ongton. Yeah. Oh yeah.
Well, yeah. Tell Mr. Russell about that. I'm glad you mentioned that.
He told me, Mr. Long, this fellow here, told me that his brother wrote Sophisticated Lady.

And I know once Barney Bigard told me that Duke, as he called him, had bought several of those tunes from Lorenzo Tio. Tio. That's right. Because Tio went up there with Piron to New York. That's right. And stayed there a few years after Piron came back.
And he sold it to Duke Ellington. Sophisticated Lady and there's something about a mood.
A mood indigo.
Mood indigo.
That's what Barney mentioned that one, I think. Yeah. My name is on there as one of the composers now, Duke and somebody else. Uh-huh. But Barney did tell me that himself.
Well, he told me that this man wrote those two mood indigo this long. Sophisticated Lady too.
Yeah. You're sure that was one of the titles?
Oh, I'm positive about Sophisticated Lady. He told me. Now, he's, he's, he's, um, Tio, but I can't remember his race name. He lives, uh,
That's a tall one, isn't he?
Wait, let me ask my son. He might be able to tell me.
He lives on London between talking and voice, I believe. Yeah, I think so. Is that a son of Lorenzo? Lorenzo?
Lorenzo had one daughter called Rose. Yeah, but his first name.
There's still some of the Tio's living here. People have told me that I never found him.
Yeah, I just found out, I think that his brother is an uncle. They live on London there. Louie.
That's it. Well, no, I want to know where he's living. Oh, Louie. Louie. Louie. Louie.
Louie. His name is Louie. His last name is Tio then too. Louie Tio.
And the one that wrote's kiss-killed lady is, he's dead. Yes, that is Lorenzo.
Lorenzo. Lorenzo.
That was my teacher.
He lived right on London. Talk to him. Oh yeah. Uh huh. Is that a son or a nephew then of your teacher?

Louie Tio. Louie Tio is Lorenzo's nephew or brother. That's his brother. His brother. That's what I said Louie. That's what I said Louie. That's what I said Louie had to be his nephew or his brother. Because I know him when I see him, he's a tall fella. Yeah. He looks a little bit like Tio. Uh huh. But he don't have that beautiful black hat like Tio. You got nice hat, but Tio has beautiful black hat.
Yes, he had very pretty black hat. I remember seeing the pictures of him.
Uh huh.

Well, he was the one who told me about it. And he is the one that has this book that I told you about. Oh yeah. I can't remember if it's National Foundation or what it is, but it was in the early 40's.
We'll try to find him then. It's over on London. We'll find him right now.
Yeah.

We'll find it. Arrange to interview him too if possible. We'll find it. We'll find it. Where's the phone book? I can give you his address if you like. Right by the desk. Right by the desk. I never thought I'd look it up in the phone book to see if there's any Tio. Well, no.

He's not even listed Tio. It would be listed as Long. It's under Long. Long. He lives with his sister-in-law, I think, or brother-in-law, or some relative. Oh, I see. And you would find it under Long.
I wonder if you ever heard your father mention the name of Dark Age, George Park Hill. Oh, yes. Quite famous. Yes.
And, uh, uh, Bechet, they have a fellow named Bechet. I knew him very well, Sidney.
My daddy played with him too. He still has a brother, I think, living uptown. I was trying to find him soon. He has uptown?
